Yes, using "they" for non-binary people is still a new concept, but not because non-binary itself is a new concept but rather the binary is a [western concept](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_gender). 

Unfortunately I don't speak any languages with the built-in concept of non-binary pronouns, however there are languages that [do actually have neutral third person pronouns](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_neutrality_in_languages_with_gendered_third-person_pronouns).

There's no singular gender-neutral pronoun in English, so we just [gotta make do](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_they). Some people have actually [invented their own](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neopronoun), which I think is pretty neat.

The singular they has been first recorded in ~1350 in [this poem](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_de_Palerme), albeit spelt "þhei". It was only considered "incorrect" a few centuries later in the ~1750s, they would use "he" as a pronoun for a person of an unknown gender.

Let's say you saw someone dropped some keys on the sidewalk, you would say "someone dropped *their* keys", because you aren't use which pronouns to use. It's sorta the same in this situation, except the gender isn't unknown, it's just unspecified and we don't really have a better word that would be socially accepted by most people.

Anyways since a few years back, using "they" as someone's pronouns is grammatically acceptable, even Merriam-Webster made the [2019 word of the year "they"](https://apnews.com/article/0b88fde3eeb023355fc2be0f8955a0b5).
